metadata.title: On Scalable Video Streaming over Cognitive Radio Cellular and Ad Hoc Networks

nodes.name: tile
nodes.statement: Note that a time slot and channel combination, termed a {\em tile}, is the minimum unit for resource allocation.
nodes.genus: a time slot and channel combination
differentia: the minimum unit for resource allocation

nodes.name: false alarm and miss detection
nodes.statement: Two types of sensing errors may occur during the sensing process. A {\em false alarm} may lead to waste a spectrum opportunity and a {\em miss detection} may causes collision with primary users.
nodes.statement_short: The two spectrum-sensing error types: a false alarm wastes an opportunity, a miss detection causes collision.

nodes.name: maximum allowed collision probability and transmission probability
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma_n \in (0, 1)$ be the {\em maximum allowed collision probability} with primary users on channel $n$, and $p^{tr}_n(t)$ the {\em transmission probability} on channel $n$ for the base station in time slot $t$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: Modulation-Coding (MC) scheme
nodes.statement: We consider $M$ unique combinations of modulation and FEC schemes, termed {\em Modulation-Coding} (MC) schemes, in this paper.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.genus: combinations of modulation and FEC schemes

nodes.name: utility of a multicast user
nodes.statement: we define the utility for user $i$ in group $g$ as $U_{g,i} = \log Q_{g,i} = \log \left( Q^b_g+\beta_g R^e_g(i) \right)$, where $R^e_g(i)$ is the received enhancement layer rate of user $i$ in group $g$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: A user's utility is the log of its received PSNR.
nodes.definiendum: the utility for user $i$ in group $g$

nodes.name: effective rate of an enhancement layer
nodes.statement: During transmission, we determine the {\em effective rate} for each enhancement layer $R_g^e \leq \bar{R}^e_g$ depending on channel availability, sensing, and MC schemes.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: tile allocation vector
nodes.statement: Letting $\vec{l} = [l_{1,1}, l_{1,2}, \cdots, l_{1,M}, l_{2,1}, \cdots l_{G,M}]$ denote the {\em tile allocation vector}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: $\mbox{Inc}(g,m,i)$ (the reward of a tile)
nodes.statement: We define $\mbox{Inc}(g,m,i)$ to be the increase in the group utility function $U(g)$ after the $i$-th tile in the sub-layer using $MC_m$ is successfully decoded. It can be shown that $$ \mbox{Inc}(g,m,i) = \sum_{k=m}^M (n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) \times \log \left[ 1+\frac{\beta_gb_{g,m}}{Q_g^b+\beta_g\sum_{u=1}^{m-1}b_{g,u}l_{g,u}+(i-1)\beta_gb_{g,m}} \right]. \nonumber $$ $\mbox{Inc}(g,m,i)$ can be interpreted as the {\em reward} if the tile is successfully received.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: The utility increase, i.e. reward, obtained when the $i$-th tile of sub-layer $m$ of group $g$ is decoded.
nodes.genus: the increase in the group utility function $U(g)$
differentia: after the $i$-th tile in the sub-layer using $MC_m$ is successfully decoded

nodes.name: availability $A_m^k$ of a channel
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa_m^k$ be a threshold for spectrum access: channel $m$ is considered idle if the estimate $a_m^k$ is greater than the threshold, and busy otherwise. The availability of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, denoted as $A_m^k$, is \begin{eqnarray} A_m^k=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0, & \mbox{$a_m^k \ge \kappa_m^k$}\\ 1, & \mbox{otherwise.}\\ \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: A channel counts as available when its belief exceeds the access threshold $\kappa_m^k$.
nodes.definiendum: The availability of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, denoted as $A_m^k$

nodes.name: set $\Omega_{i,j}$ of available channels at a link
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega_{i,j}$ be the set of available channels at link $\{i,j\}$. Assuming $i \in \mathcal{U}^k$ and $j \in \mathcal{U}^{k'}$, we have \begin{eqnarray} \Omega_{i,j} = \left\{ m \left| A_m^k=0 \mbox{ and } A_m^{k'}=0 \right. \right\}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.genus: the set of available channels at link $\{i,j\}$

nodes.name: set $\mathcal{P}_l$ of feasible paths
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}_l^A$ be the set of all possible paths from $z_l$ to $d_l$. For a given delay requirement $T_{th}$, the set of feasible paths $\mathcal{P}_l$ for video session $l$ can be determined as: \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal{P}_l = \left\{ \mathcal{P} \left| \sum_{\{i,j\} \in \mathcal{P}} \; \omega_{i,j} \le T_{th}, \; \mathcal{P} \in \mathcal{P}_l^A \right. \right\}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Feasible paths are those whose accumulated link delay meets the delay bound $T_{th}$.
nodes.definiendum: the set of feasible paths $\mathcal{P}_l$ for video session $l$

nodes.name: channel scheduling and path selection index variables
nodes.statement: We define two sets of index variables. For channel scheduling, we have \begin{eqnarray} x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{at link $\{i,j\}$, if channel $m$ is} \\ & \mbox{assigned to tunnel $r$ in path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$} \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise.} \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray} For path selection, we have \begin{eqnarray} y_l^h=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{if video session $l$ selects path $\mathcal{P}_l^h \in \mathcal{P}_l$} \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise},
nodes.statement_short: Binary indicators $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ for channel-to-tunnel assignment and $y_l^h$ for path selection.

nodes.name: set $\Lambda_{i,j}$ of loss rates of available channels
nodes.statement: Define the set of loss rates of the available channels on link $\{i, j\}$ as $\Lambda_{i,j}=\{p_{i,j}^m|m \in \Omega_{i,j} \}$.
nodes.definiendum: the set of loss rates of the available channels on link $\{i, j\}$

nodes.name: Lagrangian function of Problem OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: We then introduce positive Lagrange Multipliers $e_g$ for the path selection constraints in Problem OPT-rPS and obtain the corresponding {\em Lagrangian function}: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.45in} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h F_l^h y_l^h + \sum_g e_g (1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h ( F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g ) + \sum_g e_g \nonumber \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h ( y_l^h, \mathbf{e} )+ \sum_g e_g. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The Lagrangian of OPT-rPS obtained by dualizing the path-selection constraints with multipliers $e_g$.

nodes.name: virtual tunnel
nodes.statement: In the transmission phase, the channels assigned to a video session $l$ at each link along the path form a virtual ``tunnel'' connecting source $z_l$ and destination $d_l$.
nodes.genus: the channels assigned to a video session $l$ at each link along the path

nodes.name: amplify-and-forward relaying
nodes.statement: We adopt amplify-and-forward for video transmission~\cite{Laneman04}. During the transmission phase, one transceiver of the relay node receives video data from the upstream node on one channel, while the other transceiver of the relay node amplifies and forwards the data to the downstream node on a different, orthogonal channel.
nodes.statement_short: A relay receives on one channel and re-transmits on a different orthogonal channel without storing packets.

nodes.name: Reformulation-Linearization Technique (RLT)
nodes.statement: We use the {\em Reformulation-Linearization Technique} (RLT) to obtain the LP relaxation~\cite{Kompella09}. RLT is a technique that can be used to produce LP relaxations for a nonlinear, nonconvex polynomial programming problem. This relaxation will provide a tight upper bound for a maximization problem.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
differentia: can be used to produce LP relaxations for a nonlinear, nonconvex polynomial programming problem

nodes.name: GoP delivery deadline
nodes.statement: Due to the real-time nature, we assume that each {\em group of pictures} (GOP) must be delivered during the next GOP window, which consists of $N_G$ time slots. Beyond that, overdue data from the current GOP will be useless and will be discarded.

nodes.name: synchronous slots and Markov channel occupancy
nodes.statement: We further assume that the primary systems use a synchronous slot structure as in prior work~\cite{Zhao07a, Su08}. Due to primary user transmissions, the occupancy of each channel evolves following a discrete-time Markov process, as validated by recent measurement studies~\cite{Zhao07a, Su08, Motamedi07}.

nodes.name: two transceivers per CR node
nodes.statement: As discussed, each node is equipped with two transceivers: one for receiving and the other for transmitting video data during the transmission phase. Hence a channel cannot be used to receive and transmit data simultaneously at a relay node.

nodes.name: one channel per tunnel on each link
nodes.statement: We assume that each tunnel can only include one channel on each link. When there are multiple channels available at each link along the path, a CR source node can set up multiple tunnels to exploit the additional bandwidth.

nodes.name: Utilization of a primary channel
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \eta_m^k = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \mbox{$\sum_{t=1}^T$} S_m^k(t) = \frac{1-\lambda_m^k}{1-\lambda_m^k+\mu_m^k}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Long-run busy probability of a channel from its two-state Markov transition probabilities.

nodes.name: Conditional channel availability $a_m^k(t)$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} a_m^k(t) &=& \Pr(H_0|W_i^m=\theta_i^m, \; i \in \mathcal{U}_m^k, \pi_m^k) \nonumber \\ &=& \left[ 1 + \left( \varphi_m^k \right)^{u_m^k} \left( \phi_m^k \right)^{|\mathcal{U}_m^k|-u_m^k} \frac{\Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k)}{\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k)} \right]^{-1}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Posterior probability that a channel is idle given all users' sensing results and the channel history.

nodes.name: Sensing likelihood ratios $\varphi_m^k$ and $\phi_m^k$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \varphi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=0|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=0|H_0)}=\frac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=0 \\ \phi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=1|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=1|H_0)}=\frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=1 . \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Per-observation likelihood ratios written from the false-alarm and miss-detection probabilities.

nodes.name: One-step Markov prediction of the channel state
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k) = \lambda_m^k a_m^k(t-1) + \mu_m^k \left[ 1-a_m^k(t-1) \right] \\ \Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k) = 1-\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k). \end{array} \right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Prior for the current slot obtained by pushing last slot's belief through the Markov chain.

nodes.name: Linear PSNR rate-distortion model
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} Q_l(R_l) = Q_l^b + \beta_l(R_l - R_l^b) = Q_l^0 + \beta_l R_l, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Average PSNR of a scalable video grows affinely in the total bit rate.

nodes.name: Opportunistic transmission probability
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} p^{tr}_n(t) = \left\{ \begin{array} {ll} \min \left\{ 1, \frac{\gamma_n}{1-a_n(t)} \right\}, & \mbox{ if }\; 0 \leq a_n(t) < 1 \\ 1, & \mbox{ if }\; a_n(t) =1. \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Access probability set as large as the collision cap $\gamma_n$ permits.

nodes.name: Enhancement-layer rate as a sum of sub-layer tile rates
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} R_g^e = \sum_{m=1}^M R_{g,m}^e = \sum_{m=1}^M b_{g,m} l_{g,m}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: Group utility under MC-based user classification
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} U_g = \sum_{k=1}^M(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1})\log \left( Q^b_g+\beta_g \sum_{m=1}^k R_{g,m}^e \right), \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Group utility rewritten as a sum over MC classes weighted by how many users decode each class.

nodes.name: Total system utility
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} U = \sum_{g=1}^G U_g. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: $\tau$-step belief prediction of channel availability
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \hat{a}_n(t+\tau) = (\lambda_n-\mu_n)^\tau a_n(t)+ \mu_n \frac{1-(\lambda_n-\mu_n)^\tau}{1-(\lambda_n-\mu_n)}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Closed form for the availability belief $\tau$ slots ahead.

nodes.name: Estimated number of available tiles $T_e(t)$
nodes.statement: The number of available tiles in the following $T_{est}$ time slots can be estimated as $T_e(t) = \sum_{n=1}^N\sum_{\tau=0}^{t_{min}}\hat{a}_n(t+\tau)$, where $\hat{a}_n(t+0)=a_n(t)$ and $t_{min}=\min\{T_{est}-1,T_{GoP} - (t \; \mbox{mod} \; T_{GoP})\}$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Tile budget for the next $T_{est}$ slots obtained by summing the predicted availabilities.

nodes.name: Probability of collision with primary users on a channel
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \Pr(A_m^k=0|H_1) = \hspace{-0.05in} \sum_{i \in \psi_m^k} \hspace{-0.06in} \left( \hspace{-0.06in} \begin{array}{c} |\mathcal{U}_m^k| \\ i \end{array} \hspace{-0.06in} \right) (1-\delta_m)^{|\mathcal{U}_m^k|-i}(\delta_m)^i, \hspace{-0.05in} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Binomial sum over the miss-detection patterns that make the CR users declare a busy channel idle.

nodes.name: The index set $\psi_m^k$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \psi_m^k = \left\{ i \left| \left[ 1 + \varphi_m^i\phi_m^{ | \mathcal{U}_m^k|-i} \frac{\Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k)}{\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k)} \right]^{-1} \ge \kappa_m^k \right. \right\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The idle-vote counts whose posterior clears the access threshold $\kappa_m^k$.

nodes.name: Link loss probability
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} p_{i,j} = 1 - \prod_{m \in \mathcal{M}} \; (1-p_{i,j}^m)^{I_m}, \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: End-to-end path loss probability
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} p_l^h = 1 - \prod_{\{i,j\}\in \mathcal{P}_l^h} \; (1-p_{i,j}). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Tunnel end-to-end packet loss rate
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} p_{l,h}^r = 1 - \prod_{\{i,j\} \in \mathcal{P}_l^h} \prod_{m \in \mathcal{M}} (1-p_{i,j}^m)^{x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Loss rate of a tunnel as one minus the product of per-hop success probabilities of its scheduled channels.

nodes.name: One-channel-per-link-per-tunnel constraint
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_m x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r} \le 1, \;\; \forall \; \{i,j\} \in \mathcal{P}_l^h. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Channel availability constraint
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_r\sum_m x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r} \le |\Omega_{i,j}|, \;\; \forall \; \{i,j\} \in \mathcal{P}_l^h, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Half-duplex constraint at a relay node
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \sum_r x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r} + \sum_r x_{j,k,m}^{l,h,r} \le 1, \;\; \forall \; m, l, \forall \; h \in \mathcal{P}_l, \forall \; \{i,j\} ,\{j,k\} \in \mathcal{P}_l^h. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: A channel may not be used to receive and transmit at the same relay.

nodes.name: Source-node tunnel count constraint
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_r\sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r}=n_l^h y_l^h, \;\; \forall \; h \in \mathcal{P}_l, \forall \; l. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Destination-node tunnel count constraint
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_r\sum_m x_{d'_l,d_l,m}^{l,h,r}=n_l^h y_l^h, \;\; \forall \; h \in \mathcal{P}_l, \forall \; l. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Flow conservation at a relay node
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \sum_r\sum_m x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r} = \sum_r\sum_m x_{j,k,m}^{l,h,r}, \;\; \forall \; h \in \mathcal{P}_l, \forall \; l, \forall \; \{i,j\} ,\{j,k\} \in \mathcal{P}_l^h. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: General path-selection constraint
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_l\sum_{h\in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \forall \; g. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Generic form covering both single-path routing and path disjointedness.

nodes.name: Node-disjointedness indicator $w_{l,h}^g$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} w_{l,h}^g = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{if node $g \in $ path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$} \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}, \end{array} \right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Telescoping of the utility sum into per-slot increments
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.3in} \sum_l \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(N_G)])) - \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(0)])) \nonumber \\ && \hspace{-0.45in} = \sum_t \sum_l \left\{ \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t)])) - \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])) \right\}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The GoP-horizon utility gain equals the sum of the per-slot utility increments.

nodes.name: Per-slot expected utility increment in $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$
nodes.statement:
egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.1in} \sum_l \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t)])) - \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])) 
onumber \ &=& \sum_l \log \left( 1 +  eta_l  rac{ \mbox{E}[R_l(t)] - \mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)] }{ Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])} ight) 
onumber \ &=& \sum_l\sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l} y_l^h \log \hspace{-0.025in} \left( \hspace{-0.025in} 1 \hspace{-0.025in} + \hspace{-0.025in} \sum_r \sum_m  rac{ eta_l L_p x_{z_l, z'_l, m}^{l,h,r}}{N_G T_s Q_l^{t-1}} (1-p_{l,h}^r) \hspace{-0.025in} ight) 
onumber \ &=& \sum_l\sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l}y_l^h \log \hspace{-0.025in} \left( \hspace{-0.025in} 1 \hspace{-0.025in} + \hspace{-0.025in} ho_l^t \sum_r \sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r} (1-p_{l,h}^r) \hspace{-0.025in} ight), 
onumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The per-slot increment rewritten as a log of the scheduled, loss-discounted tunnel throughput.

nodes.name: Subgradient update of the Lagrange multipliers
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} e_g(\tau+1) = \left[ e_g(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)(1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \right]^+, \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Projected subgradient step on the dual variables with step size $\alpha(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Practical step-size rule
nodes.statement: Since the optimal solution $\mathbf{e}^{\ast}$ is not known a priori, we use the following approximation in the algorithm: $\alpha(\tau)=\frac{q(\mathbf{e}(\tau))-\hat{q}(\tau)}{||G(\tau)||^2}$, where $\hat{q}(\tau)$ is the current estimate for $q(\mathbf{e}^{\ast})$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the unknown optimal dual value by the mean of the primal and dual objective values.

nodes.name: OPT-Part
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \hspace*{-0.2in} U(\vec{l}) = \sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{k=1}^M(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) \times \log \left[ Q^b_g+\beta_g \sum_{m=1}^k b_{g,m}l_{g,m} \right] \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \hspace*{-0.2in} \sum_{g=1}^G\sum_{m=1}^M l_{g,m}\le T_e \\ && \hspace*{-0.2in} \sum_{m=1}^M b_{g,m}l_{g,m} \le \bar{R}_g^e, \; g \in [1, \cdots, M] \\ && \hspace*{-0.2in} l_{g,m} \geq 0, \; m \in [1, \cdots, M], g \in [1, \cdots, G]. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Choose the per-sub-layer tile counts $l_{g,m}$ maximizing total multicast utility under the tile budget and per-video rate caps.

nodes.name: Tile scheduling expected-reward maximization
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} \;\;\; \mbox{E} [\mbox{Reward}(\vec{\xi})] = \sum_{n=1}^N c_n(t) \cdot \mbox{Inc}(\xi_n), \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Assign tiles to the $N$ channels so as to maximize the expected utility reward in a time slot.

nodes.name: Proportional-fair video quality maximization
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_l U_l(R_l) = \sum_l \log (Q_l(R_l)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the sum of log-PSNRs over the concurrent video sessions.

nodes.name: OPT-CRV
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.4in} \mbox{max:} \;\; \sum_l \hspace{-0.03in} \sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l}y_l^h \log \hspace{-0.03in} \left( \hspace{-0.03in} 1 \hspace{-0.01in} + \hspace{-0.01in} \rho_l^t \sum_r \sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r} (1 \hspace{-0.01in} - \hspace{-0.01in} p_{l,h}^r) \hspace{-0.03in} \right) \\ && \hspace{-0.4in} \mbox{subject to:} \;\;\; (\ref{eq:DefX1}) \sim (\ref{eq:PathCon}). \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Joint path selection and channel scheduling for multi-hop CR video, subject to all the tunnel, flow and hardware constraints.

nodes.name: OPT-CS (channel scheduling)
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.2in} H_l^h=\max_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_r \sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r}(1-p_{l,h}^r) \\ && \hspace{-0.2in} \mbox{subject to:} \; (\ref{eq:OneChan1})\sim(\ref{eq:IntmFlow}), \; x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r} \in \{0,1\}, \; \mbox{for all } l, h, r, m. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: On a fixed path, schedule channels to tunnels to maximize the expected number of successfully delivered tunnels.

nodes.name: OPT-PS (path selection)
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && f(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_l \sum_h F_l^h y_l^h \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \sum_l\sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \; \mbox{for all } \; g \nonumber \\ && y_l^h \in \{0,1\}, \; \mbox{for all } \; l, h. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Binary path selection maximizing $\sum_l\sum_h F_l^h y_l^h$ under the hardware/disjointedness constraints.

nodes.name: OPT-rPS (relaxed path selection)
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && f(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_l \sum_h F_l^h y_l^h \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \sum_l\sum_{h\in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \; \mbox{for all } \; g \nonumber \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The LP obtained by relaxing the binary path variables of OPT-PS to $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Lower-level Lagrangian subproblem
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \max_{0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1} \mathcal{L}_l^h(y_l^h, \mathbf{e})=F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: One decoupled per-path maximization of the Lagrangian, solved locally at each source.

nodes.name: Relaxed dual problem
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \min_{\mathbf{e} \ge 0} \;\; q(\mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h \left( \left( y_l^h \right)^{\ast}, \mathbf{e} \right) + \sum_g e_g, \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the dual function over the non-negative multipliers $\mathbf{e}$.

nodes.name: The Sequential Fixing (SF) Algorithm

nodes.statement: \hline 1 : & Initialization: tunnel $r=1$, link $\{i,j\}$'s from $z_l$ to $d_l$; \\ 2 : & {\bf if} ($|\Lambda_{i,j}|$ == 0) \\ 3 : & $\;\;$ Exit; \\ 4 : & {\bf else if} ($|\Lambda_{i,j}|$ == 1) \\ 5 : & $\;\;$ Assign the single channel in $\Lambda_{i,j}$, $m'$, to tunnel $r$; \\ 6 & $\;\;$ Check neighboring link $\{k,i\}$; \\ 7 : & $\;\;$ {\bf if} ($p_{k,i}^{m'} \in \Lambda_{k,i}$) \\ 8 : & $\;\;\;\;$ Remove $p_{k,i}^{m'}$ from $\Lambda_{k,i}$, \\ & $\;\;\;\;$ $i \leftarrow k$, $j\leftarrow i$ and go to Step 2; \\ 9 : & $\;\;$ {\bf else} \\ 10: & $\;\;\;\;$ Go to Step 13; \\ 11: & $\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 12: & {\bf else} \\ 13: & $\;\;$ Put $\Lambda_{i,j}$ in set $\Lambda_l^h$; \\ 14: & $\;\;$ {\bf if} (node $j$ is not destination $d_l$) \\ 15: & $\;\;\;\;$ $i \leftarrow j$, $j \leftarrow v$; \\ 16: & $\;\;\;\;$ Go to Step 2; \\ 17: & $\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 18: & {\bf end if} \\ 19: & {\bf while} ($\Lambda_l^h$ is not empty) \\ 20: & $\;\;$ Find the maximum value $p_{i',j'}^{m'}$ in set $\Lambda_l^h$ \\ & $\;\;$ $\{i',j',m'\}=\arg\min \{p_{i,j}^m\}$; \\ 21: & $\;\;$ Assign channel $m'$ to tunnel $r$; \\ 22: & $\;\;$ Remove set $\Lambda_{i',j'}$ from set $\Lambda_l^h$; \\ 23: & $\;\;$ Check neighboring link $\{k,i\}$ and $\{j,v\}$; \\ 24: & $\;\;$ {\bf if} ($p_{k,i}^{m'} \in \Lambda_{k,i}$ and $\Lambda_{k,i} \in \Lambda_l^h$) \\ 25: & $\;\;\;\;$ Remove $p_{k,i}^{m'}$ from $\Lambda_{k,i}$; \\ 26: & $\;\;\;\;$ {\bf if} ($\Lambda_{k,i}$ is empty) \\ 27: & $\;\;\;\;\;\;$ Exit; \\ 28: & $\;\;\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 29: & $\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 30: & $\;\;$ {\bf if} ($p_{j,v}^{m'} \in \Lambda_{j,v}$ and $\Lambda_{j,v} \in \Lambda_l^h$) \\ 31: & $\;\;\;\;$ Remove $p_{j,v}^{m'}$ from $\Lambda_{j,v}$; \\ 32: & $\;\;\;\;$ {\bf if} ($\Lambda_{j,v}$ is empty) \\ 33: & $\;\;\;\;\;\;$ Exit; \\ 34: & $\;\;\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 35: & $\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 36: & {\bf end while} \\ 37: & Compute the next tunnel: $r \leftarrow r+1$ and go to Step 2; \\ \hline

nodes.name: Greedy most-reliable-channel tunnel construction is optimal
nodes.statement: According to Theorem~\ref{th:th1}, a greedy approach, which always chooses the channel with the lowest loss rate at each link when setting up tunnels along a path, produces the optimal overall success probability. More specifically, when there is only one tunnel to be set up along a path, the tunnel should consist of the most reliable channels available at each link along the path. When there are multiple tunnels to set up along a path, tunnel 1 should consist of the most reliable channels that are available at each link; tunnel 2 should consist of the second most reliable links available at each link; and so forth.

nodes.name: Proof of Complexity and optimality bound of GRD1
nodes.statement:
(i) {\em Complexity}: In Step 4 in Table~ef{tab:GreedyAlgo1}, it takes $O(MG)$ to solve for $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$. Since each iteration assigns one tile to sub-layer $\hat{m}$ of group $\hat{g}$, it takes $T_e$ iterations to allocate all the available tiles in a GoP window. Therefore, the overall complexity of GRD1 is $O(MGT_e)$. (ii) {\em Optimality Bound}: This proof is extended from a result first shown in~\cite{Deb08} for layered videos. We first show a property of group utility $U_g(\vec{l})$, which will be used in the proof of the optimality gap. For two vectors $\vec{l}^1_g$ and $\vec{l}^2_g$, letting $\Delta = U_g(\vec{l}^1_g)-U_g(\vec{l}^2_g)$, we have  egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.2in} \Delta = \sum_{k=1}^M (n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1 +  rac{ \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m}(l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2) }{ Q^b_g + \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 } ight) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.2in} \le \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{m=1}^k (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1+  eta_g b_{g,m} / \left[ Q^b_g+\sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 ight] ight) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.2in} \le \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{m=1}^M (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1 +  eta_g b_{g,m} / \left[ Q^b_g + \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 ight] ight) 
onumber\ & & \hspace{-0.2in} = \sum_{m=1}^M (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+ \left[ U_g(\vec{l}^2_g+b_{g,m})-U(\vec{l}^2_g) ight], \end{eqnarray} where $y^+=\max \{ 0, y \}$. The first inequality is due to the concavity of logarithm functions. Next we prove the optimality bound. Let $\vec{l}_{t}$ be the output of GRD1 after $t$ iterations. Let the utility gap between the optimal solution and the GRD1 solution be $F_{t} = U(\vec{l}^{\ast}) - U(\vec{l}_{t})$, and $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)$ the argument found in Step 4 of GRD1 after $t$ iterations. We have $\vec{l}_{t} = \vec{l}_{t-1} + \vec{e}_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t)$ and  egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.1in} F_{t-1} = U(\vec{l}^{\ast})-U(\vec{l}_{t-1}) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le \sum_g\sum_m (l_{g,m}^{\ast}-l_{g,m})^{+} [U(\vec{l}_{t-1}+\vec{e}_{g,m}(t))-U(\vec{l}_{t-1})] 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le \sum_g\sum_m (l_{g,m}^{\ast}-l_{g,m})^{+} [U(\vec{l}_{t-1}+\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t))- U(\vec{l}_{t-1})]  rac{b_{g,m}+R/T_e}{b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le  rac{U(\vec{l}_t)-U(\vec{l}_{t-1})}{ b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t) + R/T_e} \sum_g\sum_m [l_{g,m}^{\ast}(b_{g,m}+R/T_e)]. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} The first inequality is due to (ef{eq:lema2}) and the second inequality follows Step 4 of GRD1. It follows (ef{eq:st1}) that $\sum_g\sum_m l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le T_e$ and $\sum_g\sum_m b_{g,m}l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le R$. We have $F_{t-1} \le (F_{t-1}-F_{t})  rac{2R}{b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}$. Solving for $F_t$, we have $F_{t}\le F_{t-1} \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ight] / (2R) ight\}$. Suppose the {\em WHILE} loop in Table~ef{tab:GreedyAlgo1} has been executed $k$ times when the solution is obtained.  egin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_{k-1} \left\{ 1-\left[b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(k)+R/T_eight] / (2R) ight\} 
onumber \ & \le & F_0 \prod_{t=1}^k \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ight] / (2R) ight\} 
onumber \ &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] ight\}^k. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} The {\em WHILE} loop exits when one or both of two constraints are violated. If $\sum_{g}\sum_{m} l_{g,m} \le T_e$ is violated, there is no tile that can be used. Therefore $k \ge T_e$ and $\sum_{t=1}^kR/T_e\ge R$. If constraint ``$A$ is not empty'' is violated, all the videos have been allocated sufficient number of tiles and will be transmitted at full rates. We have $\sum_{t=1}^k b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t) \geq R$ in this case. It follows that  egin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] ight\}^k 
onumber \ & \le & F_0 \left[ 1 - 1/(2k) ight]^k \; \le \; F_0 e^{-1/2}. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} Since $F_0=U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$, we have $U(\vec{l}_k)\ge(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$. Therefore, we conclude that the GRD1 solution is bounded by $(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$ and $U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$.

nodes.statement: Suppose there exists a pair of $i$ and $j$ where $\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) > \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)$ and $c_i(t) < c_j(t)$. We can further increase E[Reward] by switching the tile assignment, i.e., assign channel $i$ to $\xi_j$ and channel $j$ to $\xi_i$. With this new assignment, the net increase in E[Reward] is \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.3in} c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) + c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)-c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i)-c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j) \nonumber \\ & = & [c_j(t) - c_i(t)][\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) - \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)] > 0. \nonumber \end{eqnarray} Therefore E[Reward] is maximized when the $\{ \mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) \}$ and $\{c_i(t)\}$ are in the same order.

We have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 < \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2$ and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3<\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4$. Comparing the success probabilities of the channel assignment given in Theorem~\ref{th:th1} and that of the alternative assignment, we have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 + \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 =(\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1-\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2)(\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3-\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4) > 0$. The result follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Integrality of the relaxed path-selection optimum
nodes.statement: According to Fact~\ref{thm:EqualCont}, the linearized problem of OPT-PS, i.e., OPT-rPS, can be rewritten as an equality constrained problem in the following form: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \mathbf{F}'\mathbf{y} \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \mathbf{w}_j' \mathbf{y}=1, \;\; j \in \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y}^{\ast}) \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, and $\mathbf{y}$ are column vectors with elements $F_l^h$, $w_{l,h}^g$, and $y_l^h$, respectively. We apply {\em Gauss-Jordan elimination} to the constraints in (\ref{eq:EqualCons1}) to solve for $\mathbf{y}$. Since there is not sufficient number of equations, some $y_l^h$'s are free variables (denoted as $y_i^f$) and the rest are dependent variables (denoted as $y_j^d$). Assuming there are $r$ free variables, the dependent variables can be written as linear combinations of the free variables after Gauss-Jordan elimination, as \begin{equation} y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}). \end{equation} Due to Gauss-Jordan elimination and binary vectors $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, $\bar{w}_j^i$ and $\bar{b}_j$ in (\ref{eq:depdent}) are all integers. Therefore, if all the free variables $y_i^f$ attain binary values, then all the dependent variables $y_j^d$ computed using (\ref{eq:depdent}) will also be integers. Since $0 \leq y_j^d \leq 1$, being integers means that they are either 0 or 1, i.e., binaries. That is, such a solution will be feasible. Next we substitute (\ref{eq:depdent}) into problem (\ref{eq:EqualCons}) to eliminate all the dependent variables. Then we obtain a unconstrained problem with only $r$ free variables, as \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0 \end{equation} Since the free variables $y_i^f$'s take value in \{0, 1\}, this problem can be easily solved as follows. If the coefficient $\bar{F}_i > 0$, we set $y_i^f=1$; otherwise, if $\bar{F}_i < 0$, we set $y_i^f=0$. Thus (\ref{eq:GaussElimi}) achieves its maximum objective value. Once all the free variables are determined with their optimal binary values, we computes the dependent variables using (\ref{eq:depdent}), which are also binary as discussed above. Thus we obtain a feasible solution, which is optimal.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Fact to get an equality-constrained LP, Gauss-Jordan eliminate to integer-coefficient dependencies, and maximize over the binary free variables.

nodes.name: Proof of Strong duality for OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: By definition, the problems in (\ref{eq:LagFun}) and (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) are primal/dual problems. The primal problem always has an optimal solution because it is bounded. Since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem, the relaxed dual problem is also bounded and feasible. Therefore the relaxed dual problem also has an optimal solution. We have the {\em strong duality} if the primal problem is convex, which is the case here since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of the primal LP plus strong duality for convex programs.

nodes.name: Complexity count
nodes.statement: (i) {\em Complexity}: In Step 4 in Table~\ref{tab:GreedyAlgo1}, it takes $O(MG)$ to solve for $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$. Since each iteration assigns one tile to sub-layer $\hat{m}$ of group $\hat{g}$, it takes $T_e$ iterations to allocate all the available tiles in a GoP window. Therefore, the overall complexity of GRD1 is $O(MGT_e)$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the $O(MG)$ per-iteration search by the $T_e$ tile-allocating iterations.

nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: Utility-gap recursion
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the utility gap $F_t$ and bound $F_{t-1}$ by the gain of the greedy step.

nodes.name: One-step contraction
nodes.statement: The first inequality is due to (\ref{eq:lema2}) and the second inequality follows Step 4 of GRD1. It follows (\ref{eq:st1}) that $\sum_g\sum_m l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le T_e$ and $\sum_g\sum_m b_{g,m}l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le R$. We have $F_{t-1} \le (F_{t-1}-F_{t}) \frac{2R}{b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}$. Solving for $F_t$, we have $F_{t}\le F_{t-1} \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e \right] / (2R) \right\}$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Use the OPT-Part budget constraints to turn the bound into a one-step contraction on $F_t$.

nodes.name: Iterate the contraction
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the contraction over the $k$ executions of the WHILE loop.

nodes.name: Loop-exit case split
nodes.statement: The {\em WHILE} loop exits when one or both of two constraints are violated. If $\sum_{g}\sum_{m} l_{g,m} \le T_e$ is violated, there is no tile that can be used. Therefore $k \ge T_e$ and $\sum_{t=1}^kR/T_e\ge R$. If constraint ``$A$ is not empty'' is violated, all the videos have been allocated sufficient number of tiles and will be transmitted at full rates. We have $\sum_{t=1}^k b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t) \geq R$ in this case.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Case-split on which loop condition fails to lower-bound the accumulated increments by $R$.

nodes.name: Conclude the bound
nodes.statement: It follows that \begin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] \right\}^k \nonumber \\ & \le & F_0 \left[ 1 - 1/(2k) \right]^k \; \le \; F_0 e^{-1/2}. \nonumber \end{eqnarray} Since $F_0=U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$, we have $U(\vec{l}_k)\ge(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$. Therefore, we conclude that the GRD1 solution is bounded by $(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$ and $U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $U(\vec{l}_k)\ge(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$.

nodes.name: Assume a mis-ordered pair
nodes.statement: Suppose there exists a pair of $i$ and $j$ where $\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) > \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)$ and $c_i(t) < c_j(t)$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Assume a mis-ordered pair: higher reward on the less reliable channel.

nodes.name: Exchange and compute the gain
nodes.statement: We can further increase E[Reward] by switching the tile assignment, i.e., assign channel $i$ to $\xi_j$ and channel $j$ to $\xi_i$. With this new assignment, the net increase in E[Reward] is \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.3in} c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) + c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)-c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i)-c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j) \nonumber \\ & = & [c_j(t) - c_i(t)][\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) - \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)] > 0. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Swap the two assignments and compute the strictly positive net gain.

nodes.name: Conclude co-ordering
nodes.statement: Therefore E[Reward] is maximized when the $\{ \mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) \}$ and $\{c_i(t)\}$ are in the same order.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Conclude reward and success probability must be similarly ordered.

nodes.name: Switch to success probabilities
nodes.statement: Let the success probabilities on the channels be $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1=1-p_{i,j}^1$, $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2=1-p_{i,j}^2$, $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3=1-p_{j,k}^3$, and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4=1-p_{j,k}^4$. We have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 < \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2$ and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3<\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the loss rates as success probabilities and order them.

nodes.name: Factor the difference
nodes.statement: Comparing the success probabilities of the channel assignment given in Theorem~\ref{th:th1} and that of the alternative assignment, we have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 + \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 =(\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1-\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2)(\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3-\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4) > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor the difference of the two pairings into a product of two negative terms.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The result follows.

nodes.name: Apply the Fact
nodes.statement: According to Fact~\ref{thm:EqualCont}, the linearized problem of OPT-PS, i.e., OPT-rPS, can be rewritten as an equality constrained problem in the following form: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \mathbf{F}'\mathbf{y} \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \mathbf{w}_j' \mathbf{y}=1, \;\; j \in \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y}^{\ast}) \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, and $\mathbf{y}$ are column vectors with elements $F_l^h$, $w_{l,h}^g$, and $y_l^h$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Use the Fact to replace OPT-rPS by an LP with its active inequalities as equalities.

nodes.name: Gauss-Jordan elimination
nodes.statement: We apply {\em Gauss-Jordan elimination} to the constraints in (\ref{eq:EqualCons1}) to solve for $\mathbf{y}$. Since there is not sufficient number of equations, some $y_l^h$'s are free variables (denoted as $y_i^f$) and the rest are dependent variables (denoted as $y_j^d$). Assuming there are $r$ free variables, the dependent variables can be written as linear combinations of the free variables after Gauss-Jordan elimination, as \begin{equation} y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Gauss-Jordan eliminate to write the dependent $y_j^d$ over $r$ free variables.

nodes.name: Integrality of the dependents
nodes.statement: Due to Gauss-Jordan elimination and binary vectors $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, $\bar{w}_j^i$ and $\bar{b}_j$ in (\ref{eq:depdent}) are all integers. Therefore, if all the free variables $y_i^f$ attain binary values, then all the dependent variables $y_j^d$ computed using (\ref{eq:depdent}) will also be integers. Since $0 \leq y_j^d \leq 1$, being integers means that they are either 0 or 1, i.e., binaries. That is, such a solution will be feasible.
nodes.statement_short: Integer coefficients force the dependent variables binary, hence feasible.

nodes.name: Substitute and reduce
nodes.statement: Next we substitute (\ref{eq:depdent}) into problem (\ref{eq:EqualCons}) to eliminate all the dependent variables. Then we obtain a unconstrained problem with only $r$ free variables, as \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute out the dependent variables to obtain an unconstrained problem in $r$ free variables.

nodes.name: Solve the reduced problem
nodes.statement: Since the free variables $y_i^f$'s take value in \{0, 1\}, this problem can be easily solved as follows. If the coefficient $\bar{F}_i > 0$, we set $y_i^f=1$; otherwise, if $\bar{F}_i < 0$, we set $y_i^f=0$. Thus (\ref{eq:GaussElimi}) achieves its maximum objective value.
nodes.statement_short: Set $y_i^f=1$ exactly when $\bar{F}_i>0$ to maximize.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Once all the free variables are determined with their optimal binary values, we computes the dependent variables using (\ref{eq:depdent}), which are also binary as discussed above. Thus we obtain a feasible solution, which is optimal.
nodes.statement_short: Recover the dependent variables and conclude feasibility and optimality.

nodes.name: Primal/dual pair
nodes.statement: By definition, the problems in (\ref{eq:LagFun}) and (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) are primal/dual problems.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the Lagrangian and the relaxed dual as a primal/dual pair.

nodes.name: Existence of the dual optimum
nodes.statement: The primal problem always has an optimal solution because it is bounded. Since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem, the relaxed dual problem is also bounded and feasible. Therefore the relaxed dual problem also has an optimal solution.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of the primal LP gives a bounded feasible dual with an optimum.

nodes.name: Strong duality
nodes.statement: We have the {\em strong duality} if the primal problem is convex, which is the case here since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke strong duality for the LP to equate the two optimal values.

nodes.name: Subgradient equality
nodes.statement: Since $q(\mathbf{e}(\tau))$ is a linear function, we have subgradient equality, as \begin{eqnarray} q(\mathbf{e}(\tau))-q(\mathbf{e}^{\ast})= \left[ \mathbf{e}(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast} \right]'G(\tau). \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of $q$ turns the subgradient inequality into an equality.

nodes.name: Expand the squared distance
nodes.statement_short: Expand $||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)G(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}||^2$.

nodes.name: Apply the step-size condition
nodes.statement: If $\alpha(\tau)$ satisfy (\ref{eq:StepSize}), the sum of the last two terms in (\ref{eq:Inequal1}) is negative. It follows that, $||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)G(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}|| < ||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}||$.
nodes.statement_short: The step-size condition makes the correction terms negative, so the distance strictly shrinks.

nodes.name: Conclude convergence
nodes.statement: Since the projection operation is {\em nonexpansive}, we have, \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.3in} ||\mathbf{e}(\tau+1)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}|| = ||[\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)G(\tau)]^+-[\mathbf{e}^{\ast}]^+|| \nonumber \\ &\le& ||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)G(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}|| < ||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}||, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} which states the conditional convergence of the algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Non-expansiveness of the projection carries the contraction to $\mathbf{e}(\tau+1)$.

nodes.name: Notation for the infrastructure-based setting
nodes.statement: Note that in infrastructure-based CR networks and cooperative CR networks, we assume there is only one $K=1$ primary network. In infrastructure-based CR networks introduced in the section \ref{sec:cr_video_mcast}, we adopt $N$ as the number of licensed channels since $M$ is denoted as the number of modulation-coding schemes.

nodes.name: Empirical validation of the rate-distortion model
nodes.statement: We verified the model (\ref{eq:RDfun}) with several test video sequences using the MPEG-4 FGS codec and the H.264/SVC MGS codec and found it is highly accurate.

nodes.name: Single-path routing as a special case
nodes.statement: To simplify exposition, we choose at most one path in $\mathcal{P}_l$ for video session $l$. Such a single path routing constraint can be expressed as $\sum_h y_l^h \leq 1$, which is a special case of (\ref{eq:PathCon}) where $w_{l,h}^1=1$ for all $h$, and $w_{l',h}^g=0$ for all $g \neq 1$, $l' \neq l$, and $h$. We can also have $\sum_h y_l^h \leq \xi$ to allow up to $\xi$ paths for each video session. In order to achieve optimality in the general case of multi-path routing, an optimal scheduling algorithm should be designed to dispatch packets to paths with different conditions (e.g., different number of tunnels and delays).
nodes.statement_short: Single-path and $\xi$-path routing are both instances of the general path constraint.

nodes.name: Video quality is insensitive to sensing errors
nodes.statement: It is quite interesting to see that the video quality is not very sensitive to sensing errors. Even as $\epsilon_n$ is increased nine times from 10\% to 90\%, there is only 0.58 dB reduction (or a 1.5\% normalized reduction) in average PSNR when Greedy Algorithm is used.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks

nodes.name: Timescale requirements for the distributed algorithm
nodes.statement: We assume relatively large timescales for the primary network time slots, and small to medium diameter for the CR network, such that there is sufficient time for timely feedback of channel information to the video source nodes and for the distributed algorithms to converge. Otherwise, channel information can be estimated using (\ref{eq:OneStep}) based on delayed feedback, leading to suboptimal solutions. If the time slot is too short, the distributed algorithm may not converge to the optimal solution (see Fig.~\ref{fig:timeslot}).
nodes.statement_short: Convergence needs time slots long enough for feedback and for the dual iterations to settle.

nodes.name: Only the sub-layers above $MC_{m'}$ need adjusting
nodes.statement: Due to layered videos, when we increase the number of allocated tiles, we only need to consider $l_{g,m}$ for $m=m', m'+1, \cdots, M$, where $MC_{m'}$ is the highest MC scheme used in the previous time slot. Similarly, when we reduce the number of allocated tiles, we only need to consider $l_{g,m}$ for $m=m',m'+1,\cdots,M$.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: Decoding dependency restricts GRD2's search to sub-layers at or above the highest MC scheme used.

nodes.name: MGS outperforms FGS by about 2.5 dB
nodes.statement: From the figures, it can be observed that there is a gap about 2.5 dB between the H.264/SVC MGS and MPEG-4 FGS curves, which clearly demonstrates the rate-distortion efficiency of MGS over MPEG-4 FGS.

nodes.name: Trading off resource utilization against playout smoothness
nodes.statement: For optimization-driven multimedia systems, there is a trade-off between (i) grabbing all the available resource to maximize media quality and (ii) be less adaptive to network dynamics for a smooth playout. The main objective of this paper is to demonstrate the feasibility and layout the framework for video streaming over infrastructure-based CR networks, using an objective function of maximizing the overall user utility. We will investigate the interesting problem of trading off resource utilization and smoothness in our future work.
nodes.section: 4 Video over Infrastructure Based CR Networks
nodes.statement_short: How should a CR video system balance grabbing all available spectrum against a smooth playout?
